- Hello everybody, welcome
back to Altium Academy,
I'm your host, Zach Peterson.
Today we're gonna be looking at

one of the One Minute Design
Review series submissions
in much greater detail because,

this particular submission was
based on one of the designs
that we presented on this channel,
and that is our RF power amplifier design.

Now, this design submission
attempted to follow along
with the design process that we showed
in those original videos.
And if you wanna rewatch
the Power Amplifier Design video series,

go check out the playlist
linked in the video description.
For now, let's go ahead and jump in,
look at this design review submission,
and see what we can learn about Altium

and how to do these kinds
of designs correctly.
Let's get started.
(energetic upbeat music)

Now in this video, we're
gonna take a look at

one of the One Minute
Design Review submissions
from Emirhan YILBAT.
Let's take a look at his message.
Hello, Mr. Zachariah,

I would like to share
my own design with you.

I designed it according
to your YouTube video
on the Altium Academy YouTube channel,

and I want to share it
on my LinkedIn account
by tagging you.
Well, thank you for sharing it.
Is there any issue with me doing this?

You could also share it
on your YouTube shorts
if you would like to.
Have a nice day.
Well, Emirhan, thank you very much
for sending in this design.

And I would like to point out
that this particular design

is based on the RF Power
Amplifier Design module
that we showed in another video.
You can find links to the original videos
in the video description.
Now those project files in that video

are available for download if
you go to the original videos.
You can also go over to my website,
and I have a PCB design examples page,

where I host all of the
design examples that I show
in these videos.

If you just scroll down,
you'll be able to find
the 6 GHz RF Signal Generator Design.
Now on this page I have included an embed
of an Altium viewer,
and you can use that viewer to go through
and browse the design if you like.

Or of course you can just
download the files for free,

and then use them in
your own copy of Altium.

So here, let's take a
quick look at this design.
In the original files, you can see here,
we have our original design,
and it's a pretty straightforward design.
We have an input connector, we have a VCO,
then we have our power amplifier,

we have a bunch of capacitors,
we have a dual rail LDO,
and then we have our output connector

and some headers for power,
pretty straightforward.
Next, let's look at the PCB.

Here you can see what the
original PCB looks like.
Here you have our oscillator,
here we have our power amplifier,
here's our output connector.
And then here you can see
we have one of our power regulators,

and then here we have our
dual output power regulator.

Now this power regulator over
here outputs at five volts.

You can see here we have
a pretty big inductor,

and the feedback loop
could be done a bit tighter

to get back over here to
this power regulator IC.

Here in the lower right
where we have our LDO,
you can see the layout is pretty tight,

we don't have any big inductors
to deal with of course,

and then we don't have to
route the entire power rail
back over to a feedback pin

in the same way that we have
with that switching converter,
so this layout is quite a bit better.

So we do have one area
where we could improve

in this original layout, and
that is right here with U4.

Also, we would want to
consider either adding a taper,
or adding a ground cutout.

In this particular example,
I did use the ground cutout
below that pin, on that SMA connector.

So that's what the
original design looks like.

And again, you can navigate
to those original videos,

and you can get access to the
files in those original videos

or you can just head over
to the website on screen
and you can access the files there.
Now let's go ahead and take a look
at the design from Emirhan.

Here you can see the schematic
is pulled up on screen,
and for whatever reason,

the background of the
schematic has been made pink.
I guess that's personal choice,

it's not required to be
any particular color.

I know the default color is
that kind of off yellow color
that you see in all the schematics,

but you could really make
it any color that you want.

Here you can see we have
a power up procedure,
just like we had in the original design,

and pretty much everything
else looks mostly the same,

aside from changing some
capacitors here on the power rails.

Then if you go down here we
have our voltage regulator,

again, looks pretty similar
to what we had before.

We have our LEDs, we
have our dual rail LDO,

and then we have some headers
for bridging power connections

from these power supplies
over to the various pins
on the amplifier, and on this oscillator.

So this circuitry is
pretty straightforward,

and it's basically what I
presented in the original design.
Now the learning opportunities here
are not really in the schematic,
they're actually in the PCB layout.
So let's go ahead and jump in,
and see what this PCB layout looks like.
So here we have our PCB layout,

here you can see that it
has a similar form factor
as the original power amplifier,
it is just a rectangular form factor.

Here you can see we have
additional mounting holes
in the corner.

I'm not sure why we have two
mounting holes in each corner,
we've got a small one and a large one,
but that's fine I guess,

it gives you some choices to
which mounting holes you use.

And then you can see here
that we have the RF output,
we have our feed line,

and then we have our feed
line going from the oscillator
over to the power amplifier.

Here you can see that the
switching regulator is laid out
in kind of a similar way,
we have the switching inductor over here

off to the left of the
switching regulator,

and then we're routing
out from that inductor
with our five volt rail,

and then you can see
somewhere on the backside,
we then have a larger polygon that is used

for routing that five volt
rail around the board.

Now in this particular design,
there is a lot of space
that could be used for routing,
and of course there is a lot of area

where we haven't really
filled in any ground
on the bottom layer.
So I'm gonna address each of points
as best I can individually.

First thing I wanna do is take
a look at these feed lines.
So here on these feed lines,

you can see here that we have
all of this cut up ground,
going from the top layer polygon,
over to these stitching vias.

And then that continues in
through these internal layers.

Now of course here on these
internal layers you see

that we do at least get some
ground below the feed line,

but again, it is all cut
up and jagged like this.
Why do we have all of this cut up copper
around these polygons,

and why is it making these
incomplete connections
to these vias?

Well, the reason is that we
have a thermal attach rule

that is applied by default
in the design rules.
So in order to fix that,
you need to go into the design rules,

and you need to change
the thermal attached style
on your polygons.

That can be found under
the plane category,
and then the polygon connect rule.

Now what you can see
here inside the PCB rules

and constraints editor is
that the default rule settings

have been applied to the
polygon connect rule.
Now I say this often in design reviews,

you need to change a lot of
the default rule settings

in order to comply with your
manufacturer's constraints,
or with your design requirements.

And the polygon connect
rule is one of those rules
that you almost always have to change
in every single design.
Now there are a couple of ways

that you can manage this
default rule setting.

One thing that you could do is
of course create a new rule.

And in this new rule you
could then use a query,

and in that query you
would use the isvia query.

And basically that means
that this rule setting
is only going to apply to vias.
You could then use the simple option here,
and then use direct connect.

And so because this rule is
listed above the default rule,

it is going to apply
this rule first to vias,

and it's going to apply that
direct connect only to vias.
Now if we applied that, and just hit okay,

we pour all of the
polygons, what do you see?
It magically all fills in with copper.

You can see that all of that
copper that was all cut up
on all the layers

is now directly connected
over to these vias.

Now of course you can use the
query, but you don't have to.
If you just go back into the design rules,

you'll see here that we
could actually delete
the query rule.

And you'll see here that
under the default rule,

we can actually change the
constraints to advanced.

And under the advanced option,
this allows us to control

all of the thermal
attached settings globally
with a single design rule.
Now if I scroll over here to the right,

you can see here that we
have a via connection option.
Here, I can select direct connect,

here on the left, I can leave
this through hole option

as a relief connect, which
is typically the case.

And then here you can see
for your SMD pad option,

I can also toggle between direct
connect or relief connect.
So if I go ahead and do this and hit okay,
we're gonna hit yes on this dialogue box,
then we can repour everything.

And you can see here that
these thermal connections
over here on these ground pads also
have been filled in and have disappeared.

Now if I zoom out, and I pan
above the power amplifier,

you can see here we have
the output feed line.

That output feed line
now also is surrounded

by uniform copper, both below
it and on the same layer,

and you can see we have all
of those direct connections
onto these vias.

Now speaking of thermal
relief connections,
I wanna just go back here for a moment
and take a look at the SMD pads,
because originally we had the SMD pads
with a thermal connect.

So I'm gonna go ahead and
repour all the polygons

and let's take a look
at what's going on here
with these SMA connectors.
So if I take a look at the top layer,

you can see what's happening
with this SMA connector,
especially when I put it in 3D.

This SMA connector has these
sideposts that come in,
and they need to solder onto the PCB,
and they have to solder onto these pads.
But look what's going on with these pads.

These pads don't have any
solder mask pulled off of them.

You need to go in here and
you need to select these pads
and you need to open up all of those pads
so that the solder mask is cleared.

Now here in the properties
panel under the solder section,

you'll see here that there is
an option to tent these pads.

Now you never want to
tent an SMD pad because,

of course if you do that, you
can't solder anything to it.

Now you see here that there's
the option for rule expansion

and if I try to click here
on the tented checkbox,

you can see that I'm
not able to disable it.

That's because there is
a rule that is applying,
tenting to these pads.
So the simple thing to do here
is to of course put manual expansion,

and then you could put
the solder mask expansion
at for example, one or two mils.

So if I put this at two mils,
and we look at it again in 3D,

now we can see that
those pads are opened up,

and we can actually
solder this SMA connector
onto those pads.
Now the point I was gonna make
about soldering onto these pads,

also relates to the thermal
relief onto these sideposts.

Because these sideposts need
to solder to a pad here,
but this pad, as you can see,

is connected to a very
large piece of copper,
which is basically our ground plane.

Now I have soldered these
SMA edge connectors onto

much smaller boards that
didn't have the relief connect,
and I was able to do it by hand.

I had to turn up the heat
on the soldering iron

a little bit, but I was
still able to get it to work.

But on this board, you have
so much copper on four layers

and so much copper on the
top layer around these pads,

that in this case you need to
have those thermal connections
on those SMD pads.
This will allow you to keep

your soldering iron temperature
down just a little bit,

and still be able to solder
this SMA edge connector
onto the edge of this board.
Now of course as we zoom out
with all of the 3D models hidden,
you can see here that there are other pads

that are totally covered
up with solder mask.
You can see here with D1 and D2,

those are both covered
up with solder mask.

We have some areas over
here with these headers,
all of those header pins
are also covered up with solder mask.

So we've got a problem
here with the design rules,
or with our components, or both,

where a lot of these pads
are getting covered up
with solder mask.

Now we can determine the
reason this is happening
if we just go here into the design rules.
Now, inside the design rules,

you'll see here there is an
option right here under mask
for solder mask expansion.

And you can see here that this
solder mask expansion rule
is being applied to everything,

because you can see the
scope option down here
is set to all,

and then you can see here that
we have everything tented.

This rule is basically tenting
everything in your design.
So we want to go ahead and turn that off.
If we just go ahead and hit okay,

you can then see that
all of the solder mask
gets pulled back from all of those pins
and all of those vias in this design.

Now, if your intention
is only to tent the vias

in this design, this is where
you then need to use a query.
So if you go into design and rules,

you go back to that rule
I mentioned earlier,
the solder mask expansion rule,
here you can use a custom query,

and we want to create a new
rule for use with that query.

So here in this new rule
that has prior priority,

we're then gonna get
the custom query option,
and we're gonna type in isvia,
and then here with this isvia option,
we are then going to tent everything.

Once we hit okay, we've
now applied the tenting
only to the vias in this design.

But all of our other
pads, all of our SMD pads,

all of our through hole pads,
those are all opened up.
So this is very important,

always make sure that when
you go in and apply tenting,

you know which objects you
are applying the tenting to.
You can always review the design in 3D,
and just verify visually

that the tenting has
been applied correctly.
Next thing I wanna look at in U1 and U2
is the use of thermal vias.

Now you'll notice here on
the packages for U1 and U2,
that we have these large copper pads
right here in the center.
Now of course, that is a dye attached pad,

and those pads are there
for thermal dissipation.

So the best way to pull
heat off of those pads
is to of course connect those pads
to a large piece of copper.
Now if we look 2D,

you can see here that we
have a thermal attached
onto this ground pad right here.

Thermal attach will confine
heat onto an object,
and we wanna remove heat from that object.
So that means we want to eliminate
the thermal attach on this pad.

So to do that we would then
go into the copper section
in the properties panel.

And you can see here
that there is an option
for thermal relief.

We wanna actually edit this
and create a direct connect.

So once we hit okay, we can
then repour the polygons,

and you can see here that
this automatically fills in,
and it eliminates that thermal connection.
Now the other thing that we wanna do
is apply some thermal vias.

Now these thermal vias
if applied in this pad,

would need to be applied such
that you fill them with resin

during manufacturing, so you
could fill and cap those vias

so that no solder wicks
through to the backside,
or you could place them with solder mask

and stencil openings so
that you don't deposit paste
directly onto those vias.
So either approach is gonna be just fine.
Now here on U1,

you can see a couple of
things going on here.

So the first is that
this pad, pad number 41,

that's our die attached pad,
it's not connected to anything.
So it needs to be connected to ground.
Now you can do that in the schematics,

and then once you import
that into the PCB layout,
you can then apply those thermal vias

to make that connection into
the internal ground planes.

You would wanna do the
same thing on this pad,
you would wanna make sure that

if you are not going to
fill in cap those vias,
that you design the stencil mask opening,
and the solder paste layer

to ensure that you're only
depositing solder paste
in the area where you don't have any vias.
Alternatively, if you're gonna deposit

solder paste everywhere,
you would wanna make sure
that you get those via filled and capped
during manufacturing.
But before we even do any of that,

there is actually a bigger
problem with this footprint

and that is that this
footprint is incorrect.
This is a 40 pin footprint,
but if you look here in the schematic,

you'll see that this is
only a 32 pin component.

And in fact, if you go
back to the original design
and take a look at the PCB,
this is also only a 32 pin component.
That is why this feed line

is coming into the wrong
pin on this package.

So that also needs to
be fixed in this design.
Now in the schematic symbol,
you actually have a ground connection
between the die attached exposed pad,
which is pin 33 and ground.
And then we can see here in this layout,
that pin 33 is in fact connected to ground
on the same layer.
So you did that part of it correctly,

the problem is that the
pins are just indexed
to the wrong footprint.

And the last thing I wanna
look at in this design
is the layout of this switching regulator.

Now to be fair, I mentioned
at the beginning of this video

that I could improve the layout
of that switching regulator
in the original project.

And it looks like you kind
of followed my guidance
on the layout of this switching regulator.

But one thing you did here
that was pretty interesting

was you took the output
here from this inductor,

then you drew traces to
route that five volt signal,

but then you routed through
the stackup to a polygon
on the back layer.
I'm not sure why you would do that,

it makes more sense to
just draw that polygon
on the top side.

You actually have room to
draw it on the top side.

And in fact, I can go over
here and select this polygon,

and I can take that polygon
and put it onto the top layer.

Now if I go back to the top
layer, do a quick repour,

you can see here that this
polygon just appears here
on the top layer,
and then it completes that feedback loop
over here to R5 and R8.

That would mean that
none of these other vias
are going to be needed at all.

Now if this five volt
rail was going to carry

a lot more power, you could
of course take this rail,

and you could duplicate it to
other layers in the stackup,

and then put them right
on top of each other,
and then stitch them together with vias.

That would allow you to
have much more copper

to carry all that current
without creating too much heat.

Now to make this regulator
layout more compact,
there's actually just a couple
of really simple things you could do.

One thing you could do is you
could just take this inductor
and you can move it

so that it's oriented a
little bit more like this.
Doing that would allow you

to bring this five volt
connection right here,

and then you could route
that five volt output

over here to R5, you might
wanna also move R5 up,

kind of like this, and then
that would really tighten up
the placement and routing of all the lines
in this switching regulator.

Another thing you could
do is you could take C17,

you could get it a little
tighter and closer into U4.

As you move L2, you would
also wanna move C19 and C20,
so that you also maintain a tight position
between the output of that inductor,
and those output capacitors.

The last thing I would
like to note is that

it would be a good idea to
stitch together the top side
and internal copper using stitching vias.

Now to do that, you can just
use the stitching via tool.
To do that, you would just go into tools

and then go down to via
stitching or shielding,
and use add stitching to net.

The entire point of doing
this is to ensure that
anytime there is a return current
anywhere on this top layer,

it very quickly gets down
into the reference plane.
And in order to do that,

you would then wanna place
a pretty regular array

of stitching vias going
through the entire stackup.

Now, I mentioned earlier
that there's one thing

that's missing from the back
layer, and that is of course,
copper fill on the back layer.
So if I just isolate the back layer,
most of this layer is empty.

Now the only reason that
is a problem is because,

we have the top layer
totally full of copper.

The reason we would wanna fill
the bottom layer with copper
is simply for copper balancing.
It's not that the copper reduces warpage,

it's that having balanced
copper on both halves of the PCB
is what reduces warpage.

So if you include the
copper fill on the top side,

then you also need to
include the copper fill
on the bottom side.

Easiest way to do this is
to select this polygon,

copy it to the back layer,
assign it to the ground net,
and then repour the polygon,

and then it's gonna pour over
all of those stitching vias,
and then you have a complete connection
through the entire stack up.

Now before we wrap up,
there is one last thing

I want to bring up, and that
is the pullback of copper
from the board edge.

There has been a pullback of
the copper from the board edge,
but it has basically been done manually.

The pullback here is only
six mil in the Y direction,
and 6.5 mil in the X direction.
Now that is generally not enough pullback
for most fabricators.

They're usually going
to demand that you do,
at a bare minimum, eight mil pullback,
or even a 10 mil pullback.

If you're working on a much
higher reliability design,

maybe something in automotive,
or something in aerospace,
they might demand an even bigger pullback,

something as large as
20 mil or even 30 mil.

So to automatically apply that
board outline clearance rule,

you go here into the
design rules dialogue,
and under the manufacturing section,
you'll see here there is a category
for board outline clearance.

We wanna right click
and create a new rule.
And then under that rule,
we can configure the automatic pullback
of any objects from the board edge.

If we just set a minimum
clearance of, for example, 10 mil,
we can then hit okay,
and then once we repour the polygon,

you can see here that it
automatically pulled back
that copper polygon by 10 mil.

In my opinion, this is the
absolute most convenient way
to apply board outline clearances.
Now, the last points that I wanna bring up
are the documentation for this design.
And the reason is that,

this design has controlled
impedance on it,
and it isn't RF design,

so you may have special materials
and plating requirements,

and all of those things
need to be documented
in a fabrication drawing,
or at least in a specifications document.

The standard way to do this
is in a fabrication drawing,

and we would document those
points in fabrication notes.

So to learn more about creating
and using fabrication notes,

make sure to check out the
video linked in the description
where I run over fabrication notes,

and you can even see the
standard fabrication notes
that I use in a lot of projects.
Thanks everyone for watching this video,

we always love getting your
design review submissions,
and if you do a great one,

it just might end up in
one of these deep dives.

Make sure to hit that Like
button, hit the Subscribe button,

leave your comments and questions
in the Comments section,
and last but not least,

don't forget to call
your fabricator folks,
we'll see you next time.

title: PCB Design Tips to Improve RF Power Amplifier Layout
